stories.headline: Pakistan, Saudi, Turkiye activate Mecca defence pact as Yemen war escalates
stories.title: Pakistan, Saudi, Turkiye activate Mecca defence pact as Yemen war escalates
stories.summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye have agreed to enhance military cooperation to address regional security threats. Following recent attacks by Yemen's Houthi group, the three countries will activate collective deterrence measures. The emergency meeting of the Mecca Defence Alliance in Riyadh led to this commitment. Saudi-backed forces are also launching an offensive against the Houthis in Yemen to regain control.

stories.headline: Rural porting war heats up as telcos chase users via richer retailer sops
stories.title: Rural porting war heats up as telcos chase users via richer retailer sops
stories.summary: Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio, and Vodafone Idea are racing to grab more rural users, riding a fresh wave of port-ins and a sharpened prize hunt as competition heats up
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Telecom operators are ramping up incentives for rural retailers to attract subscribers through Mobile Number Portability (MNP), signalling a shift in the competitive dynamics.

While keeping MNP payouts broadly unchanged, telcos are offering additional incentives equivalent to a month’s recharge or free demo plans for meeting specified port-in targets, according to an IIFL Capital rural survey on telecom trends.
In parts of Rajasthan, retailers received ₹299-349 per MNP after the first five port-ins, effectively equivalent to a free monthly recharge.
In rural Maharashtra, retailers are eligible for a free demo pack from a telco after completing more than three MNPs.
This marks a sharp shift from the research firm’s 2018 rural survey, when operators offered ₹200-210 per port-in only after retailers crossed 50 port-ins.
The new incentives come amid intensifying competition among Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio and Vodafone Idea (Vi) to expand their subscriber bases, industry sources told businessline.
Vi’s recent move to offer free international roaming on select plans is another sign of the changing competitive landscape, they said.

While the slowdown in incentives had earlier been attributed to the market becoming increasingly duopolistic, industry sources said the renewed push reflects operators’ efforts to protect and grow their subscriber bases.
“Increase in incentives makes sense since the market has become more competitive now that Vodafone Idea is in a better position and can be more aggressive.
The stakes are a little higher.
Almost every operator has an incentive to attract and retain more subscribers,” said Mahesh Uppal, Director, CommFirst (India).

Following the AGR (Adjusted Gross Revenue; a metric used by the DoT to calculate licence fees and spectrum usage charges owed by telecom operator) relief granted to Vi earlier this year, the operator has sought to reinvent itself in the telecom and digital spaces.

stories.headline: Did SIR deletions change Tamil Nadu assembly election’s outcome?
stories.title: Did SIR deletions change Tamil Nadu assembly election’s outcome?
stories.summary: While a businessline analysis reveals a striking geographical overlap between high voter removals and TVK victories, experts urge caution against reading it as a conspiracy
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) have stirred protests not just at the national but at the State level too.
In Tamil Nadu, DMK president and former Chief Minister MK Stalin has recently said that the deletion of several lakh voters was one of the reasons for his party’s loss.
The social media is abuzz about how TVK victory may have been aided by these deletions.
A businessline analysis of the granular data on SIR deletions and the outcome of the TN assembly elections in 2026, throws us some interesting trends.
TVK has struggled to win in constituencies where the SIR deletions were lower but has recorded more wins in constituencies where the deletions were higher.
Political analysts and experts however warn that not much should be read into these numbers.
We compared the net reduction in voter count in each constituency as per the April 2026 electoral roll with pre-SIR numbers.
Of the total 234 constituencies, 19 constituencies had lower deletions, of up to 10,000 voters.
In these, the TVK won 2 seats, the DMK 7, the AIADMK 6 and others 4.
Eighty constituencies had deletions between 10,000 to 20,000 voters.
The TVK won 22 of these constituencies, the DMK 20, the AIADMK 24 and others 14.
Sixty-six constituencies had deletions between 20,000 to 30,000.

stories.headline: Luxury car prices now 3-4 percent above pre-GST level, says Mercedes India head
stories.title: Luxury car prices now 3-4 percent above pre-GST level, says Mercedes India head
stories.summary: Luxury car prices in India are now 3 to 4 percent higher than they were before last year’s tax cuts, Mercedes-Benz India Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Santosh Iyer said on Monday, even as mass market prices remain below those levels.The price hikes haven't deterred buyers. India’s largest luxury carmaker sold 5,422 vehicles in the July-September quarter, up 6 percent from 5,119 a year earlier and 17 percent higher than the April-June quarter, making it the German carmaker’s best quarter in India. Sales for January-September rose about 8 percent to 15,190 units from 14,132, also a record.Iyer said sentiment has softened in the past two weeks because of weak capital markets, but he hasn’t yet seen any effect on car purchases.The broader industry, however, has been growing much faster than the luxury segment following last year’s Goods & Services Tax (GST) cuts.Overall car sales have grown in double digits every single month since the government cut GST on cars in September 2025.Also Read: Powertrains of thought: Mercedes-Benz's all-new modelThe reason is price hikes, feels Iyer.“Mass market prices are still below GST levels, whereas luxury car prices have gone up by 3 to 4 percent compared to the GST level,” Iyer told Forbes India. “There is a big gap.”Over the past four years, Mercedes’s average selling price has risen by about 40 percent—from Rs60 lakh to Rs1 crore today—alongside annual volume growth of 8 to 10 percent. “So, when you look at the overall business, it’s still a very strong performance, if you look at the structure and volume together.”The luxury segment depends heavily on imports, and currency swings are partially passed on to buyers. But affluent buyers give luxury automakers greater pricing power, allowing them to push through increases with less impact on demand compared to mass market carmakers.Mercedes has raised prices three times this year, in January, April and on October 1. The company has earlier said it aims for increases of about 2 percent each quarter.Rivals BMW and Audi, too, have raised prices to offset the rise in input costs.For Mercedes, the order book is strong enough and the company doesn’t expect the October increase to dent festive season demand. “Customers were told in advance and could buy in September or October,” Iyer said.Also Read: Mercedes-Benz will bring plug-in hybrids to India: MD Santosh IyerDemand outpacing supplySales could have been higher if it had more cars to sell, Iyer said.Mercedes started October with a stock that’s among the lowest since the pandemic.“That is not great news” heading into the festive season, he said, though “still a good situation to be in”.The supply squeeze mirrors a challenge facing some mass market automakers, where demand has also been running ahead of production capacity.Mercedes’s entry-level electric vehicle (EV), the CLA, which was launched in April has drawn more than 1,000 orders, but supply constraints have pushed deliveries to March or April next year.Iyer said there was a wave of replacement demand from buyers who bought cars after Covid and are now three to four years into ownership.Price increases hit first-time buyers harder than replacement customers, but about 80 percent of cars are bought on finance where the company offered EMI holidays and low interest rates. “A price rise adds only Rs500-1,000 to a monthly installment,” he said.Iyer kept his full-year guidance at single-digit growth. “It’s better to be a bit conservative in terms of outlook,” he said, citing market swings and supply constraints.On India’s new Corporate Average Fuel Economy (Cafe) norms, Iyer said the approach of favouring no single technology is the right one. “We should let the consumer decide,” he said. The rules give EVs a multiplier of 3 and plug-in hybrids 2.5.The carmaker, which reignited the conversation around plug-in hybrids in India with the launch of an S-Class plug-in hybrid earlier this year, is set to launch its first plug-in in the Mercedes-Maybach range in India later on Monday.

The company has earlier said it aims for increases of about 2 percent each quarter.
Rivals BMW and Audi, too, have raised prices to offset the rise in input costs.

Mercedes’s entry-level electric vehicle (EV), the CLA, which was launched in April has drawn more than 1,000 orders, but supply constraints have pushed deliveries to March or April next year.
Iyer said there was a wave of replacement demand from buyers who bought cars after Covid and are now three to four years into ownership.
“A price rise adds only Rs500-1,000 to a monthly installment,” he said.

“It’s better to be a bit conservative in terms of outlook,” he said, citing market swings and supply constraints.
On India’s new Corporate Average Fuel Economy (Cafe) norms, Iyer said the approach of favouring no single technology is the right one.
“We should let the consumer decide,” he said.
The rules give EVs a multiplier of 3 and plug-in hybrids 2.5.

The carmaker, which reignited the conversation around plug-in hybrids in India with the launch of an S-Class plug-in hybrid earlier this year, is set to launch its first plug-in the Mercedes-Maybach range in India later on Monday.

stories.headline: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road ahead
stories.title: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road ahead
stories.summary: India and the United States have reached a “plateau” in their trade negotiations, beyond which further give-and-take would be “very very difficult”, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said at the Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Monday.“The agreements and negotiations are still ongoing, although we like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” Sitharaman said.Speaking at a session on the next generation of trade agreements, Sitharaman said the talks had been “hard and very rigorously negotiated” but remain unfinalised. She pointed to the core sticking point, which is a trade balance that favours India, leaving Washington keen to narrow the deficit and recover what it sees as past losses.She added that tariffs, once a negotiating instrument within a framework, have been “weaponised”, while countries like India still have to negotiate and trade concessions.“Negotiation used to be the only platform through which countries could highlight the discrepancies, highlight the lopsidedness….Now the imbalance is being sought to be addressed through other means. Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it,” the finance minister said.In contrast, she held up the India-EU pact as a model. Covering roughly a quarter of global GDP and trade, India has opened 92.5 percent of tariff lines, about 97 percent by value, while the EU has opened around 99 percent by value. Sensitive sectors, such as dairy and soya for India and meat and dairy for Europe, were carefully managed, she said.Also Read: Nirmala Sitharaman: Global Economy Needs Resilience Amid UncertaintySitharaman argued the deal would boost jobs, as exports such as footwear, textiles, toys and processed components come from labour-intensive micro, small and medium enterprises, employing many women.She also said that bilateral and multilateral deals were never mutually exclusive, but that weakened institutions like the WTO had tilted the balance towards bilateral pacts. “Countries chose where multilateral [agreements] would benefit them, and there are some unique bilaterals which countries choose to have. Now the balance is somewhat built in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she added.On the Bilateral Investment Treaty of 2016, she said that India is finalising a new bilateral investment protection template to replace the 2016 model, awaiting cabinet approval.“We had had a template which was cabinet approved in 2016, which itself cancelled out the earlier one, and that became currency….That agreement now we think does not deliver much good for us. So, in the last one and a half years, I worked on a new template for a bilateral protection agreement,” she added. She expects agreements with at least three more countries by December, with Canada likely by December or early next year; Russia is among those in talks.Sitharaman also flagged the strain on food security from fertiliser disruptions. India imports about 80 percent of its requirement, selling a unit to farmers at Rs 300, though it costs Rs 3,000 to import. She said that fertiliser prices have “gone through the roof” while also being a “big challenge” for India since Covid.“Fertilisers have gone through the roof. It is just not possible for any country to sustain buying it at that level,” the minister added. Shipping disruptions and insurance costs after the war in West Asia have prompted a special shipping emergency fund.She said India’s climate commitments continue, citing rooftop solar, solar pumps and new modular nuclear reactor legislation.

stories.headline: The Legal Transformation of Jammu & Kashmir After 2019
stories.title: The Legal Transformation of Jammu & Kashmir After 2019
stories.summary: Introduction The constitutional developments of 5 August 2019 marked a watershed in the legal history of Jammu and Kashmir. Public and political discourse has largely focused on the abrogation of Article 370 and the reorganisation of the erstwhile State. For the legal community, however, the transformation has been considerably broader. The post-2019 process involved not merely a change in the constitutional relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the Union of India, but a comprehensive reconstruction of the statutory, administrative and institutional framework governing the territory. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, enacted by Parliament on 9 August 2019, provided for the reorganisation of the erstwhile State into two Union Territories: the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir with a legislature, and the Union Territory of Ladakh without a legislature. The appointed day under the Act was 31 October 2019. This was followed by an extensive process of extending Central laws, repealing or adapting existing Jammu and Kashmir legislation, restructuring institutions and modifying administrative arrangements. The result is that the legal architecture of Jammu and Kashmir today is substantially different from that which existed before August 2019. The Legal Transformation of Jammu & Kashmir After 2019: From Constitutional Exceptionalism to a Common Legal Framework Rights, Criminal Law, Judicial Review and the Road Ahead I. Women, Equality and the Changing Legal Framework: The earlier permanent-resident framework had generated considerable legal and political debate concerning the rights of women who married persons who were not permanent residents. Judicial intervention had already altered aspects of the earlier legal position before 2019. Nevertheless, the removal of the former permanent-resident constitutional framework and the introduction of a domicile-based statutory regime fundamentally changed the legal context in which such questions are considered. Many issues that were previously examined through the lens of Jammu and Kashmir-specific constitutional doctrines can now be analysed primarily through: Article 14; Article 15; Article 16; other constitutional guarantees of equality and non-discrimination; and applicable statutory rights. The broader significance is that questions of equality are increasingly situated within the general constitutional framework applicable across India. II. Language and Cultural Recognition: Legal transformation has also extended into the field of language policy. The Jammu and Kashmir Official Languages Act, 2020 established a new statutory framework concerning official languages in the Union Territory. The recognition of languages such as Dogri and Kashmiri, alongside the existing linguistic framework, is significant from both legal and cultural perspectives. Constitutional integration need not imply cultural homogenisation. India’s constitutional framework accommodates national unity alongside linguistic and cultural diversity. For Jammu and Kashmir, therefore, the challenge is to strengthen constitutional integration while preserving and promoting the linguistic and cultural traditions associated with Dogri, Kashmiri, Gojri, Pahari and other regional communities. III. From the Ranbir Penal Code to the New Criminal Laws: Few areas demonstrate the speed of the post-2019 legal transition more clearly than criminal law. For decades, Jammu and Kashmir operated under its own substantive criminal code, the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC). Following reorganisation, the Indian Penal Code (IPC) became applicable in place of the RPC. That phase itself proved transitional. With the nationwide criminal-law reforms coming into force on 1 July 2024, the IPC was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS). Similarly, the criminal-procedure and evidence regimes transitioned to the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), subject to their respective transitional provisions. Consequently, within roughly five years, criminal-law practitioners in Jammu and Kashmir had to navigate three distinct stages: RPC → IPC → BNS and corresponding procedural and evidentiary changes. The consequences are not merely academic. For offences committed during different periods, courts must determine the applicable substantive law and transitional provisions. Constitutional safeguards against retrospective penal legislation remain fundamental. The transition has therefore required significant retraining and adaptation by: Advocates; Judges; Prosecutors; Police authorities; and Other criminal-justice institutions. IV. The Judiciary and the Continuing Role of Judicial Review: Institutional transformation does not eliminate the central role of judicial review. The High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh remains a crucial constitutional institution for protecting fundamental and legal rights and scrutinising administrative action. Its role becomes particularly important during periods of legislative transition. When laws are repealed or adapted, institutions reorganised, and new statutory regimes introduced, questions concerning interpretation and transitional rights inevitably arise. Constitutional courts consequently perform an essential function: they provide the legal bridge between legislative transformation and the rule of law. Integration into a common constitutional framework cannot mean unrestricted administrative authority. On the contrary, constitutionalism requires that administrative power remain subject to legality, reasonableness, judicial review and constitutional rights. The success of legal integration must therefore be measured not simply by uniformity of legislation, but by the quality of constitutional protection available to citizens. V. The Supreme Court and the Constitutional Status of Article 370: The constitutional controversy surrounding Article 370 ultimately reached a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India. In its judgment delivered in December 2023, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional measures concerning the cessation of the operation of Article 370. The judgment therefore became the most significant judicial pronouncement concerning the constitutional changes introduced in 2019. Yet the legal transformation cannot be understood solely through the Article 370 litigation. By the time the Supreme Court delivered its judgment, an extensive statutory, administrative and institutional framework had already developed in Jammu and Kashmir. The legal debate had therefore moved beyond the question of Article 370 to the much broader consequences of constitutional and statutory integration. VI. What Has Really Changed? The transformation since 2019 can ultimately be understood as a shift in the starting point of legal analysis. Before 2019, lawyers dealing with Central legislation frequently had to ask: “Does this Central law apply to Jammu and Kashmir?” Today, the starting assumption is substantially different. Jammu and Kashmir operates predominantly within the general constitutional and parliamentary framework of India, subject to the laws and provisions specifically applicable to the Union Territory. That change in the lawyer’s starting point itself demonstrates the scale of the transformation. The significance of 2019 therefore lies not merely in the constitutional amendment or reorganisation of territory, but in the creation of an entirely different legal environment. VII. Integration Must Ultimately Mean Justice: The post-2019 legal transformation is undeniably historic. But legislation should not be evaluated merely by counting the number of laws extended, adapted or repealed. The ultimate purpose of law is justice. The more important questions are therefore practical: Has governmental decision-making become more accountable? Has access to justice improved? Have vulnerable communities received stronger legal protection? Have women and historically disadvantaged groups obtained greater equality? Are tribal communities receiving effective implementation of statutory rights? Are administrative authorities applying the new laws fairly and consistently? Do ordinary citizens understand and experience their rights more effectively? These questions require objective assessment. Supporting constitutional integration does not require abandoning critical scrutiny of administration. Indeed, constitutionalism demands the opposite. A mature legal order must combine constitutional integration with accountability, transparency, equality and effective judicial remedies. VIII. The Road Ahead: From Integration to Consolidation: August 2019 did not merely close one constitutional chapter in Jammu and Kashmir. It opened an entirely new legal era. The transformation extends across: Constitutional law; Administrative law; Criminal law; Land law; Service jurisprudence; Tribal rights; Political representation; Language policy; and Institutional governance. For the legal profession, the transformation has been particularly profound. The contemporary Jammu and Kashmir lawyer must understand not only the historical State laws but also: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019; Adaptation orders; Central legislation; The new criminal laws; Post-reorganisation rules and regulations; and The evolving constitutional jurisprudence of the Supreme Court and High Court. The next challenge is therefore no longer merely legal integration. It is legal consolidation. Laws must be accessible and clearly understood. Transitional ambiguities must be resolved. Administrative authorities must apply statutes consistently. Citizens must be made aware of their rights. Courts must continue to protect constitutional freedoms. Conclusion The legal transformation of Jammu and Kashmir after August 2019 represents one of the most significant constitutional and statutory reorganisations in contemporary India. Its consequences extend far beyond Article 370. The transformation has altered the constitutional structure, reorganised institutions, changed the statutory framework, introduced a new domicile regime, restructured land laws, expanded the application of Central legislation, strengthened the framework of tribal rights and political representation, changed the criminal-law regime and placed Jammu and Kashmir within a substantially more common constitutional framework. For the legal profession, the transition has created opportunities. The challenge is to reconcile historical laws and transitional provisions with the new legal order. The opportunity is to build a legal system that is more accessible, predictable and rights-oriented. Ultimately, the success of the post-2019 transformation cannot be measured simply by whether Jammu and Kashmir now possesses statutes similar to those applicable elsewhere in India. opening: Introduction The constitutional developments of 5 August 2019 marked a watershed in the legal history of Jammu and Kashmir.
Public and political discourse has largely focused on the abrogation of Article 370 and the reorganisation of the erstwhile State.
body: For the legal community, however, the transformation has been considerably broader.

The post-2019 process involved not merely a change in the constitutional relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the Union of India, but a comprehensive reconstruction of the statutory, administrative and institutional framework governing the territory.

The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, enacted by Parliament on 9 August 2019, provided for the reorganisation of the erstwhile State into two Union Territories: the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir with a legislature, and the Union Territory of Ladakh without a legislature.
The appointed day under the Act was 31 October 2019.

This was followed by an extensive process of extending Central laws, repealing or adapting existing Jammu and Kashmir legislation, restructuring institutions and modifying administrative arrangements.
The result is that the legal architecture of Jammu and Kashmir today is substantially different from that which existed before August 2019.
After 2019: From Constitutional Exceptionalism to a Common Legal Framework Rights, Criminal Law, Judicial Review and the Road Ahead.

I. Women, Equality and the Changing Legal Framework: The earlier permanent-resident framework had generated considerable legal and political debate concerning the rights of women who married persons who were not permanent residents.
Judicial intervention had already altered aspects of the earlier legal position before 2019.

Nevertheless, the removal of the former permanent-resident constitutional framework and the introduction of a domicile-based statutory regime fundamentally changed the legal context in which such questions are considered.

Many issues that were previously examined through the lens of Jammu and Kashmir-specific constitutional doctrines can now be analysed primarily through: Article 14; Article 15; Article 16; other constitutional guarantees of equality and non-discrimination; and applicable statutory rights.
The broader significance is that questions of equality are increasingly situated within the general constitutional framework applicable across India.
Language and Cultural Recognition: Legal transformation has also extended into the field of language policy.
The Jammu and Kashmir Official Languages Act, 2020 established a new statutory framework concerning official languages in the Union Territory.
The recognition of languages such as Dogri and Kashmiri, alongside the existing linguistic framework, is significant from both legal and cultural perspectives.
Constitutional integration need not imply cultural homogenisation.
India’s constitutional framework accommodates national unity alongside linguistic and cultural diversity.

For Jammu and Kashmir, therefore, the challenge is to strengthen constitutional integration while preserving and promoting the linguistic and cultural traditions associated with Dogri, Kashmiri, Gojri, Pahari and other regional communities.
From the Ranbir Penal Code to the New Criminal Laws: Few areas demonstrate the speed of the post-2019 legal transition more clearly than criminal law.
For decades, Jammu and Kashmir operated under its own substantive criminal code, the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC).
Following reorganisation, the Indian Penal Code (IPC) became applicable in place of the RPC.
That phase itself proved transitional.
With the nationwide criminal-law reforms coming into force on 1 July 2024, the IPC was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).

Similarly, the criminal-procedure and evidence regimes transitioned to the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), subject to their respective transitional provisions.
Consequently, within roughly five years, criminal-law practitioners in Jammu and Kashmir had to navigate three distinct stages: RPC → IPC → BNS and corresponding procedural and evidentiary changes.
The consequences are not merely academic.
For offences committed during different periods, courts must determine the applicable substantive law and transitional provisions.
Constitutional safeguards against retrospective penal legislation remain fundamental.
The transition has therefore required significant retraining and adaptation by: Advocates; Judges; Prosecutors; Police authorities; and Other criminal-justice institutions.
The Judiciary and the Continuing Role of Judicial Review: Institutional transformation does not eliminate the central role of judicial review.
The High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh remains a crucial constitutional institution for protecting fundamental and legal rights and scrutinising administrative action.
Its role becomes particularly important during periods of legislative transition.
When laws are repealed or adapted, institutions reorganised, and new statutory regimes introduced, questions concerning interpretation and transitional rights inevitably arise.
Constitutional courts consequently perform an essential function: they provide the legal bridge between legislative transformation and the rule of law.
Integration into a common constitutional framework cannot mean unrestricted administrative authority.
On the contrary, constitutionalism requires that administrative power remain subject to legality, reasonableness, judicial review and constitutional rights.
The success of legal integration must therefore be measured not simply by uniformity of legislation, but by the quality of constitutional protection available to citizens.
V. The Supreme Court and the Constitutional Status of Article 370: The constitutional controversy surrounding Article 370 ultimately reached a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India.
In its judgment delivered in December 2023, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional measures concerning the cessation of the operation of Article 370.
The judgment therefore became the most significant judicial pronouncement concerning the constitutional changes introduced in 2019.
Yet the legal transformation cannot be understood solely through the Article 370 litigation.
By the time the Supreme Court delivered its judgment, an extensive statutory, administrative and institutional framework had already developed in Jammu and Kashmir.
The legal debate had therefore moved beyond the question of Article 370 to the much broader consequences of constitutional and statutory integration.
What Has Really Changed?
The transformation since 2019 can ultimately be understood as a shift in the starting point of legal analysis.
Before 2019, lawyers dealing with Central legislation frequently had to ask: “Does this Central law apply to Jammu and Kashmir?” Today, the starting assumption is substantially different.
Jammu and Kashmir operates predominantly within the general constitutional and parliamentary framework of India, subject to the laws and provisions specifically applicable to the Union Territory.
That change in the lawyer’s starting point itself demonstrates the scale of the transformation.
The significance of 2019 therefore lies not merely in the constitutional amendment or reorganisation of territory, but in the creation of an entirely different legal environment.
Integration Must Ultimately Mean Justice: The post-2019 legal transformation is undeniably historic.
But legislation should not be evaluated merely by counting the number of laws extended, adapted or repealed.
The ultimate purpose of law is justice.
The more important questions are therefore practical: Has governmental decision-making become more accountable?
Has access to justice improved?
Have vulnerable communities received stronger legal protection?
Have women and historically disadvantaged groups obtained greater equality?
Are tribal communities receiving effective implementation of statutory rights?
Are administrative authorities applying the new laws fairly and consistently?
Do ordinary citizens understand and experience their rights more effectively?
These questions require objective assessment.
Supporting constitutional integration does not require abandoning critical scrutiny of administration.
Indeed, constitutionalism demands the opposite.
A mature legal order must combine constitutional integration with accountability, transparency, equality and effective judicial remedies.
The Road Ahead: From Integration to Consolidation: August 2019 did not merely close one constitutional chapter in Jammu and Kashmir.
It opened an entirely new legal era.

The transformation extends across: Constitutional law; Administrative law; Criminal law; Land law; Service jurisprudence; Tribal rights; Political representation; Language policy; and Institutional governance.
For the legal profession, the transformation has been particularly profound.

The contemporary Jammu and Kashmir lawyer must understand not only the historical State laws but also: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019; Adaptation orders; Central legislation; The new criminal laws; Post-reorganisation rules and regulations; and The evolving constitutional jurisprudence of the Supreme Court and High Court.
The next challenge is therefore no longer merely legal integration.
It is legal consolidation.
Laws must be accessible and clearly understood.
Transitional ambiguities must be resolved.
Administrative authorities must apply statutes consistently.
Citizens must be made aware of their rights.
Courts must continue to protect constitutional freedoms.
Conclusion.
The legal transformation of Jammu and Kashmir after August 2019 represents one of the most significant constitutional and statutory reorganisations in contemporary India.
Its consequences extend far beyond Article 370.

The transformation has altered the constitutional structure, reorganised institutions, changed the statutory framework, introduced a new domicile regime, restructured land laws, expanded the application of Central legislation, strengthened the framework of tribal rights and political representation, changed the criminal-law regime and placed Jammu and Kashmir within a substantially more common constitutional framework.
For the legal profession, the transition has created opportunities.
The challenge is to reconcile historical laws and transitional provisions with the new legal order.
The opportunity is to build a legal system that is more accessible, predictable and rights-oriented.
Ultimately, the success of the post-2019 transformation cannot be measured simply by whether Jammu and Kashmir now possesses statutes similar to those applicable elsewhere in India.
It must be measured by whether those laws deliver the constitutional promise of equality, dignity, accountability, access to justice and the rule of law.
Constitutional integration was the beginning.
Equal and effective justice must be its ultimate destination.
(The author is an advocate and can be reached at: parimokshseth@gmail.com ).

stories.headline: Why India's trade policy makes imports cheaper than manufacturing
stories.title: Why India's trade policy makes imports cheaper than manufacturing
stories.summary: In November 2024, a low-carbon ferrochrome (LCFeCr) plant inside the Andhra Pradesh Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) at Atchutapuram near Visakhapatnam fell silent. The SEZ unit, run by TUF Metallurgical Pvt Ltd, had roughly Rs 25 crore invested in it, a dedicated 4,000 KVA power connection, an annual capacity of about 7,200 tonnes, and around 150 workers, directly or indirectly, on its rolls. Its product, LCFeCr, is an alloy used in stainless steel, special alloy steel and foundry applications. While demand for the product persisted, the plant had been priced out of its own supply chain by the government's customs rules.The central issue was how India's trade policy and customs framework determines the duties applicable when a product or mineral is "imported" or "exported" from an Indian SEZ to the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), or under India's preferential trade agreements (PTAs) with another country. This case highlights inconsistencies embedded in India's trade policy design. It is a story that extends beyond a single plant, company or metal. Similar contradictions could emerge in sectors ranging from chemicals and electronics to textiles.TUF's SEZ unit needed chrome concentrate, its primary raw material, from mines in Odisha for use within another Indian SEZ, an entirely domestic transfer. The fifth proviso to Rule 27(1) of the SEZ Rules purported to require payment of the same 30 percent export duty ordinarily applicable when chrome ore or concentrate is exported from India, even when the material moved from the DTA into an Indian SEZ, on the assumption that any movement into an SEZ qualifies as an "export" for duty purposes.On September 18, 2025, the Andhra Pradesh High Court, in TUF Metallurgical Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (W.P. No. 15528 of 2024), struck down the fifth proviso to Rule 27(1) of the SEZ Rules, 2006, as ultra vires the SEZ Act, 2005. Despite the ruling, consignments already procured from Odisha remained outside the SEZ gate for weeks because customs officials were not informed of the court's decision. The episode highlighted that a legal victory does not automatically guarantee a smooth supply chain.That, however, was only the first challenge.Under Section 30 of the SEZ Act, any finished good that an SEZ unit sells into the rest of India is treated, for customs purposes, as if it were imported from abroad and taxed on its full value, including the labour, power and processing that went into making it.For TUF's ferrochrome, this translates into a customs duty of about 5.5 percent, including the social welfare surcharge. The duty may appear modest until the India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which came into force on June 1, 2026, is taken into account. Under the CEPA, qualifying LCFeCr manufactured in Oman, including in an Omani free zone where the applicable Rules of Origin are satisfied, can enter India at zero customs duty under tariff item 72024900. By contrast, an Indian-made LCFeCr product cleared from an SEZ to an Indian customer ordinarily faces an effective customs duty of 5.5 percent before IGST. The result is that the Indian manufacturing unit is taxed at both ends of its value chain.A further competitive asymmetry arises from the fact that Oman's Free Zone allows duty-free import of chrome concentrate, a key raw material for LCFeCr production, from Pakistan. The material can subsequently be used in ferrochrome manufacturing. Indian producers, meanwhile, face a 200 percent import duty on products from Pakistan.The India-Oman CEPA does not address such inconsistencies. An Oman-based producer can source duty-free raw materials from Pakistan, while Indian manufacturers face substantially higher import duties. The issue goes beyond conventional tariff liberalisation and raises questions about the adequacy of the CEPA's Rules of Origin, anti-circumvention provisions and India's domestic tariff structure for critical industrial inputs.India could address this through stricter product-specific scrutiny of Rules of Origin, closer examination of the economic transformation occurring in Oman under the CEPA framework and, where economically justified, rationalisation of domestic tariffs on chrome concentrate.Also Read: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road aheadThe incentive structure is reversedThe consequences are not merely theoretical. They raise significant concerns about commercial viability and public interest.If one considers both factors together, the incentive structure is effectively reversed. An entrepreneur deciding where to establish the next chrome-alloy furnace may conclude that an Indian SEZ is no longer the most competitive location. In an Indian SEZ, the finished product is taxed as an import when sold domestically. In contrast, the same product can be manufactured in a free zone in Oman, such as the Sohar Free Zone, and shipped into India duty-free.India has, in effect, created a policy architecture in which manufacturing domestically can become more expensive than manufacturing abroad and importing the final product back into the country, a classic inverted duty structure. This disadvantage may be compounded by fiscal incentives, including corporate tax holidays or exemptions available, subject to applicable conditions, in competing free-zone jurisdictions such as Oman.With around 150 direct and indirect jobs dependent on the Atchutapuram unit, the case illustrates the practical consequences of this policy dilemma. Downstream stainless steel and alloy steel manufacturers would likely have preferred sourcing from a nearby Indian supplier, benefiting from shorter lead times and easier technical coordination rather than relying on a longer import chain.Instead, the outcome has been a loss of employment, capacity utilisation, supplier relationships, tax collections and investor confidence. It also affects government revenues because an idle plant, power connection and industrial land generate neither GST nor income tax, nor the wider economic activity associated with a functioning factory.A fix without undoing trade agreementsThese individual policies are not unreasonable in isolation. Duty-free imports of inputs and capital goods for authorised SEZ operations make sense if the unit is expected to export. Taxing SEZ goods sold into India as imports also has a rationale if the SEZ is legally treated as being outside the customs territory. Similarly, a zero-duty concession to Oman can be justified as part of a trade agreement that provides reciprocal market access.The problem is that these policies have not been adequately evaluated in combination. As the TUF case demonstrates, their cumulative effect is to create an incentive to relocate manufacturing activity that India is fully capable of undertaking domestically, contrary to the objectives of Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat.The policy solution does not require dismantling the Oman CEPA or other PTAs, abandoning the export-oriented character of SEZs, or providing ferrochrome producers with permanent subsidies. Rather, it requires a narrower and more targeted approach. SEZ units selling into India should pay customs duty only on the duty foregone on imported inputs, rather than on the value added through domestic labour, power and manufacturing processes.India already follows this principle under two comparable schemes: Export Oriented Undertakings (EOUs) and the MOOWR scheme (Manufacturing and Other Operations in Warehouse), which allows manufacturers to import raw materials and capital goods without paying customs duty upfront.In both cases, the customs duty foregone on imported inputs is recovered when goods are sold domestically, instead of taxing the finished product as a notional import. There appears to be no significant administrative obstacle to extending the same principle to SEZ clearances into the DTA.The government has already taken a limited and temporary step in this direction by introducing a concessional-duty window for eligible SEZ-to-DTA clearances between April 1, 2026 and March 31, 2027 through Notification No. 11/2026-Customs dated March 31, 2026. However, TUF's Low Carbon Ferro Chrome, classified under tariff item 72024900, does not appear to be covered by the notification.More fundamentally, the March 2026 notification could be viewed as an acknowledgement that the existing SEZ-to-DTA duty framework may require corrective intervention in certain circumstances. A more durable solution would be to incorporate a duty-recovery mechanism directly into the SEZ Act for all eligible products rather than relying on ad hoc exemptions. Such an approach would provide the predictability required in a competitive trading environment.Also Read: Nirmala Sitharaman: Global Economy Needs Resilience Amid UncertaintyEnsuring a level playing fieldA more fundamental intervention would ensure that products manufactured in Indian SEZs receive treatment comparable to products imported under India's PTAs when they enter the DTA, subject to appropriate safeguards. This would create a level playing field for domestic manufacturing.Indian SEZ-produced goods should not face higher duties when entering the DTA than identical or comparable products manufactured abroad and imported under a PTA. Such an approach would strengthen the competitiveness of India's manufacturing base and support the objectives of Make in India, while preserving the integrity of the SEZ framework and India's preferential trade commitments.India is negotiating and signing free trade and preferential trade agreements at a faster pace than at any point in its history. Yet tariff concessions are being layered onto an existing framework of domestic exemptions, SEZ regulations and customs rules. The combined effect of new concessions and existing regulations requires much closer scrutiny before future agreements are concluded.For manufacturing growth and investor confidence, one question should be asked consistently: Do newly negotiated tariff concessions, when combined with existing rules, make it cheaper to import a finished product than to manufacture it in India or an Indian SEZ?Where the answer is yes, as it currently is for ferrochrome, the issue is worth fixing before the furnace goes cold, not after.Prof. Rajesh Babu Ravindran, Professor of Law and Public Policy at IIM Calcutta.

They raise significant concerns about commercial viability and public interest.
If one considers both factors together, the incentive structure is effectively reversed.

This disadvantage may be compounded by fiscal incentives, including corporate tax holidays or exemptions available, subject to applicable conditions, in competing free-zone jurisdictions such as Oman.
With around 150 direct and indirect jobs dependent on the Atchutapuram unit, the case illustrates the practical consequences of this policy dilemma.

It also affects government revenues because an idle plant, power connection and industrial land generate neither GST nor income tax, nor the wider economic activity associated with a functioning factory.

These individual policies are not unreasonable in isolation.
Taxing SEZ goods sold into India as imports also has a rationale if the SEZ is legally treated as being outside the customs territory.
Similarly, a zero-duty concession to Oman can be justified as part of a trade agreement that provides reciprocal market access.
The problem is that these policies have not been adequately evaluated in combination.

As the TUF case demonstrates, their cumulative effect is to create an incentive to relocate manufacturing activity that India is fully capable of undertaking domestically, contrary to the objectives of Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
The policy solution does not require dismantling the Oman CEPA or other PTAs, abandoning the export-oriented character of SEZs, or providing ferrochrome producers with permanent subsidies.
Rather, it requires a narrower and more targeted approach.
SEZ units selling into India should pay customs duty only on the duty foregone on imported inputs, rather than on the value added through domestic labour, power and manufacturing processes.

India already follows this principle under two comparable schemes: Export Oriented Undertakings (EOUs) and the MOOWR scheme (Manufacturing and Other Operations in Warehouse), which allows manufacturers to import raw materials and capital goods without paying customs duty upfront.
In both cases, the customs duty foregone on imported inputs is recovered when goods are sold domestically, instead of taxing the finished product as a notional import.
There appears to be no significant administrative obstacle to extending the same principle to SEZ clearances into the DTA.

The government has already taken a limited and temporary step in this direction by introducing a concessional-duty window for eligible SEZ-to-DTA clearances between April 1, 2026 and March 31, 2027 through Notification No. 11/2026-Customs dated March 31, 2026.
However, TUF's Low Carbon Ferro Chrome, classified under tariff item 72024900, does not appear to be covered by the notification.
More fundamentally, the March 2026 notification could be viewed as an acknowledgement that the existing SEZ-to-DTA duty framework may require corrective intervention in certain circumstances.
A more durable solution would be to incorporate a duty-recovery mechanism directly into the SEZ Act for all eligible products rather than relying on ad hoc exemptions.
Such an approach would provide the predictability required in a competitive trading environment.
Ensuring a level playing field.

A more fundamental intervention would ensure that products manufactured in Indian SEZs receive treatment comparable to products imported under India's PTAs when they enter the DTA, subject to appropriate safeguards.
This would create a level playing field for domestic manufacturing.
Indian SEZ-produced goods should not face higher duties when entering the DTA than identical or comparable products manufactured abroad and imported under a PTA.

Such an approach would strengthen the competitiveness of India's manufacturing base and support the objectives of Make in India, while preserving the integrity of the SEZ framework and India's preferential trade commitments.
India is negotiating and signing free trade and preferential trade agreements at a faster pace than at any point in its history.
Yet tariff concessions are being layered onto an existing framework of domestic exemptions, SEZ regulations and customs rules.
The combined effect of new concessions and existing regulations requires much closer scrutiny before future agreements are concluded.

For manufacturing growth and investor confidence, one question should be asked consistently: Do newly negotiated tariff concessions, when combined with existing rules, make it cheaper to import a finished product than to manufacture it in India or an Indian SEZ?
Where the answer is yes, as it currently is for ferrochrome, the issue is worth fixing before the furnace goes cold, not after.

article_sentences: Underlining the need to take preventive measures against sexual offences, the Supreme Court on Monday (October 5, 2026) asked the Delhi.
Police to set up 24-hour monitoring cells for continuous surveillance of vulnerable areas.
The court also asked the police to strengthen patrolling, particularly around educational institutions and public spaces.

A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran observed that the mere installation of CCTV cameras in public spaces would serve little purpose without continuous monitoring to detect suspicious activity and enable a swift police response.
“When we are talking about surveillance through CCTV cameras, how far will they help curb crimes if there is no continuous monitoring at different war rooms?
The cameras will help you in catching hold of the culprit, but how will you prevent such crimes?
There has to be a cell — a 24-hour cell — which keeps monitoring what is happening,” the Bench observed.
The court was hearing a suo motu case concerning a spate of sexual assault incidents involving minors and women in the Delhi-National Capital Region.
It had earlier indicated that it intended to fix accountability on authorities entrusted with preventing crime and protecting vulnerable persons.
